claim: Only a small percentage of patients show response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI).
source: However, only a small percentage of patients show response to ICI, and there is an unmet need for biomarkers that will identify patients who are more likely to respond to immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about ICI response rates.

claim: Tumor immunogenicity is primarily determined by tumor antigenicity and antigen presentation efficiency.
source: The fundamental basis for ICI response is the immunogenicity of a tumor, which is primarily determined by tumor antigenicity and antigen presentation efficiency.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework in the abstract.

claim: TIGS combines tumor mutational burden (TMB) and an expression signature of the antigen processing and presenting machinery (APM).
source: Here, we propose a method to measure tumor immunogenicity score (TIGS), which combines tumor mutational burden (TMB) and an expression signature of the antigen processing and presenting machinery (APM).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: TIGS showed improved performance compared to TMB and other known prediction biomarkers for ICI response in correlation with pan-cancer ICI objective response rates (ORR).
source: In both correlation with pan-cancer ICI objective response rates (ORR) and ICI clinical response prediction for individual patients, TIGS consistently showed improved performance compared to TMB and other known prediction biomarkers for ICI response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results section.

claim: TIGS showed improved performance compared to TMB and other known prediction biomarkers for ICI response in ICI clinical response prediction for individual patients.
source: In both correlation with pan-cancer ICI objective response rates (ORR) and ICI clinical response prediction for individual patients, TIGS consistently showed improved performance compared to TMB and other known prediction biomarkers for ICI response.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the results section.

claim: Most tumor types show response rates below 40% to PD-1 inhibition.
source: Most tumor types show response rates below 40% to PD-1 inhibition, and the response rates of each tumor type are reported to be correlated with the tumor mutational burden (TMB) of that tumor type (Yarchoan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yarchoan et al., 2017.

claim: The response rates of each tumor type are correlated with the tumor mutational burden (TMB) of that tumor type.
source: Most tumor types show response rates below 40% to PD-1 inhibition, and the response rates of each tumor type are reported to be correlated with the tumor mutational burden (TMB) of that tumor type (Yarchoan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yarchoan et al., 2017.

claim: PD-L1 expression affects ICI effectiveness.
source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herbst et al., 2014 and Shukuya and Carbone, 2016.

claim: TMB affects ICI effectiveness.
source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rizvi et al., 2015 and Snyder et al., 2014.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tang et al., 2016.

source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).

source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowell et al., 2018 and Zaretsky et al., 2016.

source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ayers et al., 2017.

source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davoli et al., 2017.

source: Multiple factors are reported to affect ICI effectiveness, including: PD-L1 expression (Herbst et al., 2014; Shukuya and Carbone, 2016), TMB (Rizvi et al., 2015; Snyder et al., 2014), DNA mismatch repair deficiency (Le et al., 2015), the degree of cytotoxic T cell infiltration (Tang et al., 2016), mutational signature (Miao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), antigen presentation defects (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016), interferon signaling (Ayers et al., 2017), tumor aneuploidy (Davoli et al., 2017) and T-cell signatures (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2018.

claim: Tumors of very low or no immunogenicity will not respond to therapeutic strategies that enhance the immune response.
source: Theoretically, tumors of very low or no immunogenicity will not respond to therapeutic strategies that enhance the immune response.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle.

claim: ICI can only be used to treat tumors that have sufficient immunogenicity.
source: Hence, ICI can only be used to treat tumors that have sufficient immunogenicity.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference from the principle of tumor immunogenicity.

claim: Enhancing tumor immunogenicity can potentially transform an immunotherapy-non-responsive tumor into an immunotherapy-responsive tumor.
source: Furthermore, enhancing tumor immunogenicity can potentially transform an immunotherapy-non-responsive tumor into an immunotherapy-responsive tumor.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis based on the concept of tumor immunogenicity.

claim: Tumor immunogenicity is determined by the tumor cell itself and is also influenced by factors related to the tumor microenvironment.
source: In theory, tumor immunogenicity is determined by the tumor cell itself, and is also influenced by factors related to the tumor microenvironment, such as the functioning of professional antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells (DCs) (Mellman and Steinman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mellman and Steinman, 2001.

claim: Professional antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells influence tumor immunogenicity.
source: In theory, tumor immunogenicity is determined by the tumor cell itself, and is also influenced by factors related to the tumor microenvironment, such as the functioning of professional antigen-presenting cells like dendritic cells (DCs) (Mellman and Steinman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mellman and Steinman, 2001.

claim: Fundamental determinants of tumor immunogenicity include tumor antigenicity and antigen processing and presenting efficiency.
source: Fundamental determinants of tumor immunogenicity include tumor antigenicity, and antigen processing and presenting efficiency (Blankenstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blankenstein et al., 2012.

claim: Antigen presentation defects contribute to ICI-response failure.
source: Antigen presentation defects have already been shown to contribute to ICI-response failure (Chowell et al., 2018; Zaretsky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chowell et al., 2018 and Zaretsky et al., 2016.

claim: APM score (APS) was calculated from the mRNA expression status of APM genes using a gene set variation analysis (GSVA) method.
source: To measure antigen processing and presenting efficiency systematically, we applied a gene set variation analysis (GSVA) method to generate an antigen processing and presenting machinery (APM) score (APS) (Hänzelmann et al., 2013), which was calculated from the mRNA expression status of APM genes.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, supported by a citation to Hänzelmann et al., 2013.

claim: Cell surface presentation of peptides by MHC class I molecules is critical to CD8+ T-cell mediated adaptive immune responses against tumors.
source: Cell surface presentation of peptides by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecules is critical to CD8+ T-cell mediated adaptive immune responses, including those against tumors.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: The generation and loading of peptides onto MHC class I molecules require the functioning of the APM.
source: The generation and loading of peptides onto MHC class I molecules require the functioning of the APM.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge.

claim: APM process involves peptide generation and trimming in the proteasome.
source: Several steps are involved in this process, including: 1) peptide generation and trimming in the proteasome; 2) peptide transport; 3) assembly of the MHC class loading complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); and 4) antigen presentation on cell surface (Leone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leone et al., 2013.

claim: APM process involves peptide transport.
source: Several steps are involved in this process, including: 1) peptide generation and trimming in the proteasome; 2) peptide transport; 3) assembly of the MHC class loading complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); and 4) antigen presentation on cell surface (Leone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leone et al., 2013.

claim: APM process involves assembly of the MHC class loading complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Several steps are involved in this process, including: 1) peptide generation and trimming in the proteasome; 2) peptide transport; 3) assembly of the MHC class loading complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); and 4) antigen presentation on cell surface (Leone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leone et al., 2013.

claim: APM process involves antigen presentation on cell surface.
source: Several steps are involved in this process, including: 1) peptide generation and trimming in the proteasome; 2) peptide transport; 3) assembly of the MHC class loading complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER); and 4) antigen presentation on cell surface (Leone et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leone et al., 2013.

claim: The efficiency of antigen processing and presentation is one determinant of tumor immunogenicity.
source: The efficiency of antigen processing and presentation is one determinant of tumor immunogenicity.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle underlying the study.

claim: The following genes were selected for APM quantification: PSMB5, PSMB6, PSMB7, PSMB8, PSMB9, PSMB10, TAP1, TAP2, ERAP1, ERAP2, CANX, CALR, PDIA3, TAPBP, B2M, HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C.
source: On the basis of a review paper about APM (Leone et al., 2013), the following genes were selected for quantification: PSMB5, PSMB6, PSMB7, PSMB8, PSMB9, PSMB10, TAP1, TAP2, ERAP1, ERAP2, CANX, CALR, PDIA3, TAPBP, B2M, HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, based on Leone et al., 2013.

claim: There is large variance in APS across TCGA cancer types.
source: The boxplot in Figure 1A shows large variance in APS across TCGA cancer types, which uncovers significant distinction in antigen-processing and -presenting efficiency among different cancer types.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is significant distinction in antigen-processing and -presenting efficiency among different cancer types.
source: The boxplot in Figure 1A shows large variance in APS across TCGA cancer types, which uncovers significant distinction in antigen-processing and -presenting efficiency among different cancer types.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The APS quantified in this study is highly correlated with a previous expression signature of seven APM genes.
source: This analysis is similar to a previous study of seven APM genes (Şenbabaoğlu et al., 2016) whose expression signature is highly correlated with the APS quantified in this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Şenbabaoğlu et al., 2016.

claim: No significant correlations can be observed between APS and PHBR scores.
source: However, no significant correlations can be observed between APS and PHBR scores (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), probably because these two methods capture different information about antigen presentation: PHBR are based on MHC genotype information, whereas APS are based on information about the expression of antigen-presentation genes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PHBR are based on MHC genotype information, whereas APS are based on information about the expression of antigen-presentation genes.
source: However, no significant correlations can be observed between APS and PHBR scores (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), probably because these two methods capture different information about antigen presentation: PHBR are based on MHC genotype information, whereas APS are based on information about the expression of antigen-presentation genes.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the lack of correlation between APS and PHBR.

claim: APS is associated with cancer patients' survival in some cancer types.
source: Univariate Cox regression analyses suggest that APS is associated with cancer patients' survival, and some are statistically significant (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Meta-analysis with pan-cancer hazard ratio values suggests that APS do not associate with prognosis.
source: Meta-analysis with pan-cancer hazard ratio values suggests that APS do not associate with prognosis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Several gene signatures, especially interferon alpha/gamma response, were found to be enriched in most TCGA cancer types with high APS.
source: In results from hallmark gene sets, several gene signatures (especially interferon alpha/gamma response) were found to be enriched in most TCGA cancer types with high APS, suggesting that high APS is strongly associated with the interferon alpha/gamma signaling pathway (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: High APS is strongly associated with the interferon alpha/gamma signaling pathway.
source: In results from hallmark gene sets, several gene signatures (especially interferon alpha/gamma response) were found to be enriched in most TCGA cancer types with high APS, suggesting that high APS is strongly associated with the interferon alpha/gamma signaling pathway (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GSEA results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Interferon gamma regulates APM gene expression.
source: Interestingly, interferon gamma was reported to regulate APM gene expression (Beatty and Paterson, 2001; Ikeda et al., 2002), which is consistent with this observation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beatty and Paterson, 2001 and Ikeda et al., 2002.

claim: There is significant correlation between APM score and IIS in 8949 cancer samples.
source: Significant associations between APS and IIS at both the level of cancer types and the level of individual patients were observed (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is significant correlation between APM score and IIS in different cancer types.
source: Significant associations between APS and IIS at both the level of cancer types and the level of individual patients were observed (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The gene list for APS calculation did not overlap with the gene list for IIS calculation.
source: The gene list for APS calculation did not overlap with the gene list for IIS calculation.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological detail to support the independence of the two measures.

claim: Different cancer types show different prognosis in relation to high TMB.
source: Different cancer types show different prognosis in relation to high TMB (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Meta-analysis including all TCGA cancer types suggests that patients with high TMB tend to have poor prognosis.
source: Meta-analysis including all TCGA cancer types suggests that patients with high TMB tend to have poor prognosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: TMB reflects tumor antigenicity and predicted improved survival after immunotherapy.
source: TMB reflects tumor antigenicity and predicted improved survival after immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TMB.

claim: In cancer patients not treated with immunotherapy, high TMB tends to be associated with poor prognosis, probably because tumors accumulate mutations during progression as a result of genome instability.
source: However, in cancer patients not treated with immunotherapy, high TMB tends to be associated with poor prognosis, probably because tumors accumulate mutations during progression as a result of genome instability, and consequently, high TMB is usually associated with late-stage cancer.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observed association between high TMB and poor prognosis.

claim: High TMB is usually associated with late-stage cancer.
source: However, in cancer patients not treated with immunotherapy, high TMB tends to be associated with poor prognosis, probably because tumors accumulate mutations during progression as a result of genome instability, and consequently, high TMB is usually associated with late-stage cancer.
evidence: This is stated as an inference to explain the association between high TMB and poor prognosis.

claim: Several types of immune cells, including cytotoxic cells, show strong correlation with APS values.
source: Several types of immune cells, including cytotoxic cells, show strong correlation with APS values (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: TMB and IIS show relatively weak intercorrelation.
source: TMB and IIS show relatively weak intercorrelation (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The significant correlation between APS and IIS could be due to the immune response coordinated by interferon signaling regulating both APS and IIS.
source: The significant correlation between APS and IIS could be due to the following reasons: first, the immune response coordinated by interferon signaling could regulate both APS and IIS; and second, the immunogenicity contributed by APS could stimulate immune response.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for the observed correlation.

claim: The significant correlation between APS and IIS could be due to the immunogenicity contributed by APS stimulating immune response.
source: The significant correlation between APS and IIS could be due to the following reasons: first, the immune response coordinated by interferon signaling could regulate both APS and IIS; and second, the immunogenicity contributed by APS could stimulate immune response.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative explanation for the observed correlation.

claim: Tumor immunogenicity is determined by two factors: the antigenicity of tumor cells and the processing and presentation of tumor antigens.
source: Tumor immunogenicity is determined by two factors: the antigenicity of tumor cells and the processing and presentation of tumor antigens.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical framework for TIGS calculation.

claim: These two factors (antigenicity and antigen presentation) are independent and are both required for tumor immunogenicity determination.
source: These two factors are independent, and are both required for tumor immunogenicity determination.
evidence: This is stated as a theoretical principle underlying TIGS calculation.

claim: Non-synonymous tumor mutation and the production of neoantigens can elicit immune response.
source: Non-synonymous tumor mutation and, consequently, the production of neoantigens can elicit immune response (Schumacher and Schreiber, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schumacher and Schreiber, 2015.

claim: Log-based TMB values show a Gaussian distribution.
source: Pan-cancer TMB distribution was analyzed, and log-based TMB values were found to show a Gaussian distribution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 (which is actually Figure 3—figure supplement 1 based on the images).

claim: Log(TMB) shows linear correlation with pan-cancer immunotherapy ORR.
source: In addition, a previous study had already indicated that log(TMB) shows linear correlation with pan-cancer immunotherapy ORR (Yarchoan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yarchoan et al., 2017.

claim: Cancer types with high TIGS include: skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC).
source: Cancer types with high TIGS include: skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TIGS is associated with cancer patients' survival in some cancer types.
source: Univariate Cox regression analysis suggests that TIGS is associated with cancer patients' survival, and this association is statistically significant for some cancer types (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Cox regression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Meta-analysis involving all TCGA cancer types suggested that high TIGS tends to be associated with a poor prognosis in patients not treated with immunotherapy.
source: Meta-analysis involving all TCGA cancer types suggested that high TIGS tends to be associated with a poor prognosis in patients not treated with immunotherapy (Figure 3B), which may be due to a mechanism that is the same as that which leads to high TMB.
evidence: This is supported by meta-analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The correlation coefficient between APS and ORR is 0.42 (p=0.038).
source: The correlation coefficients between APS and ORR and between TMB and ORR were 0.42 (p=0.038) and 0.71 (p=6.8e-5), respectively (Figure 4), suggesting that 18% and 50% of the difference in the ORR across cancer types could be explained by APS and TMB, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The correlation coefficient between TMB and ORR is 0.71 (p=6.8e-5).
source: The correlation coefficients between APS and ORR and between TMB and ORR were 0.42 (p=0.038) and 0.71 (p=6.8e-5), respectively (Figure 4), suggesting that 18% and 50% of the difference in the ORR across cancer types could be explained by APS and TMB, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 18% of the difference in the ORR across cancer types could be explained by APS.
source: The correlation coefficients between APS and ORR and between TMB and ORR were 0.42 (p=0.038) and 0.71 (p=6.8e-5), respectively (Figure 4), suggesting that 18% and 50% of the difference in the ORR across cancer types could be explained by APS and TMB, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the correlation coefficient (R²=0.42²≈0.18).

claim: 50% of the difference in the ORR across cancer types could be explained by TMB.
source: The correlation coefficients between APS and ORR and between TMB and ORR were 0.42 (p=0.038) and 0.71 (p=6.8e-5), respectively (Figure 4), suggesting that 18% and 50% of the difference in the ORR across cancer types could be explained by APS and TMB, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the correlation coefficient (R²=0.71²≈0.50).

claim: The correlation coefficient between TIGS and ORR is 0.78 (p=5.4e-6).
source: The correlation coefficient between TIGS and ORR is 0.78 (p=5.4e-6) (Figure 4C), indicating that 60% of the difference in ORR could be explained by TIGS.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 60% of the difference in ORR could be explained by TIGS.
source: The correlation coefficient between TIGS and ORR is 0.78 (p=5.4e-6) (Figure 4C), indicating that 60% of the difference in ORR could be explained by TIGS.
evidence: This is calculated from the correlation coefficient (R²=0.78²≈0.60).

claim: TIGS performs better than TMB or APS in correlations with immunotherapy ORR.
source: These pan-cancer ORR analyses imply that TIGS performs better than TMB or APS in correlations with immunotherapy ORR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analyses comparing TIGS, TMB, and APS.

claim: TIDE outperforms known immunotherapy biomarkers — TMB, PD-L1 expression, and interferon gamma gene expression signature — in predicting the response to immunotherapy in melanoma and lung cancer.
source: TIDE outperforms known immunotherapy biomarkers — TMB, PD-L1 expression, and interferon gamma gene expression signature — in predicting the response to immunotherapy in melanoma and lung cancer (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2018.

claim: TIGS consistently achieved better performance than TMB in all three ICI datasets.
source: When compared to the widely used ICI-response biomarker TMB, TIGS consistently achieved better performance in all three ICI datasets (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The predictive power of TIGS was comparable to that of TIDE in the two melanoma datasets.
source: The predictive power of TIGS was comparable to that of TIDE in the two melanoma datasets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ROC curve analysis comparing TIGS and TIDE.

claim: TIDE failed to predict response to immunotherapy in urothelial cancer.
source: However, TIDE failed to predict response to immunotherapy in urothelial cancer, so TIGS showed better performance in the urothelial cancer dataset (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TIGS outperforms other immunotherapy biomarkers that are based on gene expression profiling, including IIS, IFNG, ISG.RS, IFNG.GS and CD8, in all three datasets.
source: TIGS also outperforms other immunotherapy biomarkers that are based on gene expression profiling, including IIS, IFNG, ISG.RS, IFNG.GS and CD8, in all three datasets (Figure 5D–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by AUC comparison shown in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: APS itself shows improved or similar prediction power when compared to other gene-expression-profiling-based biomarkers.
source: Interestingly, APS itself also shows improved or similar prediction power when compared to other gene-expression-profiling-based biomarkers (Figure 5D–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by AUC comparison shown in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression profiles of randomly selected genes failed to predict immunotherapy response in all three datasets.
source: The expression profiles of randomly selected genes (named 'APSr' in Figure 5D–F), which were used as a negative control, failed to predict immunotherapy response in all three datasets.
evidence: This is supported by AUC values shown in Figure 5D-F for the negative control.

claim: TIGS-High patients showed significantly better survival curves than TIGS-Low patients in all three ICI datasets.
source: However, TIGS-High patients showed significantly better survival curves than TIGS-Low patients in all three ICI datasets (Figure 5J–L).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 5J-L.

claim: In all three available datasets, TIGS outperforms TMB and other biomarkers that are based on gene-expression profiling (TIDE, IFNG etc.) in accurately predicting clinical response to immunotherapy and in pan-cancer applicability.
source: These analyses suggest that in all three available datasets, TIGS outperforms TMB and other biomarkers that are based on gene-expression profiling (TIDE, IFNG etc.) in accurately predicting clinical response to immunotherapy and in pan-cancer applicability.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the analyses comparing TIGS with other biomarkers.

claim: TIGS capture two key aspects of tumor immunogenicity, antigen presentation and tumor antigenicity.
source: TIGS capture two key aspects of tumor immunogenicity, antigen presentation and tumor antigenicity, which could be the reason for its improved performance in ICI-response prediction when compared to known biomarkers.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for TIGS's improved performance.

claim: The formula for TIGS calculation can point to a new way to transform some ICI-non-responsive tumors into responsive tumors by enhancing the tumor immunogenicity.
source: Furthermore, our formula for TIGS calculation can point to a new way to transform some ICI-non-responsive tumors into responsive tumors by enhancing the tumor immunogenicity.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the TIGS framework.

claim: Interferon signaling is the top gene signature associated with APS-High.
source: Our GSEA indicates that interferon signaling is the top gene signature associated with APS-High, and interferon signaling has been reported to influence APM gene expression (Beatty and Paterson, 2001; Ikeda et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA results and citations to Beatty and Paterson, 2001 and Ikeda et al., 2002.

claim: Antigen presentation may be enhanced by stimulating interferon signaling in patients who are initially not responsive to ICI.
source: We may enhance antigen presentation by stimulating interferon signaling in patients who are initially not responsive to ICI, especially in cancer types that have low APS, such as prostate cancer and breast cancer.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative therapeutic strategy.

claim: Breast cancer and prostate cancer have usual TMB but fairly low ICI-response rates, probably because of low APS.
source: Breast cancer and prostate cancer have usual TMB but fairly low ICI-response rates, probably because of low APS; renal clear cell carcinoma has good ICI response rate, possibly as a result of high APS.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data based on the TIGS framework.

claim: Renal clear cell carcinoma has good ICI response rate, possibly as a result of high APS.
source: Breast cancer and prostate cancer have usual TMB but fairly low ICI-response rates, probably because of low APS; renal clear cell carcinoma has good ICI response rate, possibly as a result of high APS.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data based on the TIGS framework.

claim: The linear correlation formula ORR = 21.4 × TIGS – 2.7 can be used to make hypotheses with respect to the ORR in tumor types for which anti–PD-1 therapy has not been explored.
source: Furthermore, our linear correlation formula — ORR = 21.4 × TIGS – 2.7 (this formula is based on the data in Figure 4C) — can be used to make hypotheses with respect to the ORR in tumor types for which anti–PD-1 therapy has not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the TIGS correlation with ORR.

claim: A clinically meaningful ORR of 12.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 8.8% to 15.8%) is anticipated for uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) on the basis of a median TIGS of 0.7.
source: For example, we anticipate a clinically meaningful ORR of 12.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 8.8% to 15.8%) for uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) on the basis of a median TIGS of 0.7.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the linear correlation formula derived from the data.

claim: Other factors including tumor germline antigen, copy number variation status, tumor purity and intra-tumor heterogeneity should be considered to enable more accurate measurement of the antigenicity of tumor cells.
source: First, other factors including tumor germline antigen, copy number variation status, tumor purity and intra-tumor heterogeneity should also be considered to enable more accurate measurement of the antigenicity of tumor cells.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction for improving TIGS.

claim: For quantifying antigen presentation efficiency, APM protein expression and function assessment will be more accurate than APM mRNA expression measurement.
source: Second, for quantifying antigen presentation efficiency, APM protein expression and function assessment will be more accurate than APM mRNA expression measurement.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction for improving TIGS.

claim: Other factors that influence TIGS should be considered, including the function of professional antigen presentation cells (dendritic cells for example) in the immune microenvironment.
source: Third, other factors that influence TIGS should also be considered, including the function of professional antigen presentation cells (dendritic cells for example) in the immune microenvironment.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction for improving TIGS.

claim: This manuscript primarily focused on the cytosolic or endogenous neoantigen presentation pathway mediated by MHC class I.
source: This manuscript primarily focused on the cytosolic or endogenous neoantigen presentation pathway mediated by MHC class I.
evidence: This is stated as a scope limitation of the study.

claim: A sex difference in the predictive power of TMB has been reported recently in lung cancer.
source: In addition, a sex difference in the predictive power of TMB has been reported recently in lung cancer (Wang et al., 2019b; Wang et al., 2019c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2019b and Wang et al., 2019c.

claim: TIGS is tumor cell-based and is distinct from immunophenoscore or T-cell dysfunction and exclusion signature.
source: TIGS is tumor cell-based, and is distinct from the recent immunotherapy biomarkers immunophenoscore (Charoentong et al., 2017) or T-cell dysfunction and exclusion signature (Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated to distinguish TIGS from other biomarkers, with citations to Charoentong et al., 2017 and Jiang et al., 2018.

claim: Immunophenoscore and T-cell dysfunction and exclusion signature are based on tumor immune microenvironment.
source: Both of these ICI biomarkers are based on tumor immune microenvironment.
evidence: This is stated to contrast with TIGS, which is tumor cell-based.

claim: As a tumor inherent biomarker, TIGS can be used for predicting immunotherapy response and can point ways to manipulate the immunogenicity of tumors.
source: As a tumor inherent biomarker, TIGS can not only be used for predicting immunotherapy response, but also point ways to manipulate the immunogenicity of tumors, and consequently the response to immunotherapy.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the utility of TIGS.

claim: About 10,000 tumors of 32 cancer types from TCGA were analyzed for pan-cancer distribution pattern of APS.
source: To explore the pan-cancer distribution pattern of APS, we analyzed about 10,000 tumors of 32 cancer types from TCGA (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: GSVA calculates the per sample overexpression level of a particular gene list by comparing the ranks of the genes in that list with those of all other genes.
source: GSVA calculates the per sample overexpression level of a particular gene list by comparing the ranks of the genes in that list with those of all other genes.
evidence: This describes the GSVA methodology.

claim: PHBR I and II scores quantify a patient's antigen presentation ability on the basis of the genotypes of their MHC class I or class II genes, respectively.
source: Patient Harmonic Best Rank (PHBR) I and II scores have recently been proposed to quantify a patient's antigen presentation ability on the basis of the genotypes of their MHC class I or class II genes, respectively (Marty Pyke et al., 2018; Marty et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marty Pyke et al., 2018 and Marty et al., 2017.

claim: TIMER results were highly correlated with the calculated IIS.
source: To further validate the calculated IIS, we performed TIMER analysis (Li et al., 2016) and found that the TIMER results were highly correlated with the calculated IIS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: TMB was defined as the number of non-synonymous alterations per megabase (Mb) of genome examined.
source: TMB was defined as the number of non-synonymous alterations per megabase (Mb) of genome examined.
evidence: This describes the definition of TMB used in the study.

claim: 38 Mb was used as the estimate of the exome size.
source: As reported previously (Chalmers et al., 2017), we used 38 Mb as the estimate of the exome size.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chalmers et al., 2017.

claim: The normalized APS is set to 0 if a loss of function mutation exists in the B2M gene.
source: The normalized APS is set to 0 if a loss of function mutation exists in the B2M gene.
evidence: This describes a specific adjustment made in the TIGS calculation methodology.

claim: 25 cancer types have both TMB and ORR values and also have transcriptome data that can be used for calculating APS.
source: In total, 28 cancer types have both TMB and ORR values, and 25 of them also have transcriptome data that can be used for calculating APS.
evidence: This describes the dataset used for pan-cancer ORR correlation analysis.

claim: Three datasets were identified for evaluating the power of TIGS to predict clinical response to ICIs: Van Allen et al. (2015), Hugo et al. (2016), and Snyder et al. (2017).
source: To evaluate the power of TIGS to predict clinical response to ICIs, we searched PubMed for ICI clinical studies for which TMB and gene transcriptome information was available for individual patients. In total, three datasets were identified after this search.
evidence: This describes the datasets used for individual patient response prediction analysis.

claim: In the Van Allen et al. (2015) dataset, 'clinical benefit' was defined using a composite end point of complete response or partial response to CTLA-4 blockade as assessed by RECIST criteria or stable disease by RECIST criteria with overall survival greater than 1 year.
source: This dataset related to CTLA-4 blockade in metastatic melanoma, and defined 'clinical benefit' using a composite end point of complete response or partial response to CTLA-4 blockade as assessed by RECIST criteria or stable disease by RECIST criteria with overall survival greater than 1 year, 'no clinical benefit' was defined as progressive disease by RECIST criteria or stable disease with overall survival less than 1 year (Van Allen et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the response criteria used in the Van Allen et al. (2015) dataset, supported by a citation.

claim: In the Hugo et al. (2016) dataset, responding tumors were derived from patients who have complete or partial responses or stable disease in response to anti-PD-1 therapy; non-responding tumors were derived from patients who had progressive disease.
source: This dataset related to anti-PD-1therapy in metastatic melanoma: responding tumors were derived from patients who have complete or partial responses or stable disease in response to anti-PD-1 therapy; non-responding tumors were derived from patients who had progressive disease (Hugo et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the response criteria used in the Hugo et al. (2016) dataset, supported by a citation.

claim: In the Snyder et al. (2017) dataset, durable clinical benefit was defined as progression-free survival >6 months.
source: This dataset related to PD-L1 blockade in urothelial cancer: durable clinical benefit was defined as progression-free survival >6 months (Snyder et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the response criteria used in the Snyder et al. (2017) dataset, supported by a citation.
